passages.text: ELECTRICITY, the operations of a very subtile fluid, which is excited by the friction of glass, amber, sealing-wax and other bodies, and causes them to attract and repel light substances.
Bodies are divided into electrics, which may be excited by friction, as glass and resin, and conductors, as metals and water, which transmit the fluid freely.
Dr Franklin has shown that lightning is the same with electricity, by drawing it from the clouds with a kite, and has taught the method of securing buildings by pointed rods of iron.
Electricity has been applied with success in medicine, in palsies, rheumatisms and other disorders.
Some philosophers suppose that the nervous fluid itself may be of the same nature with the electric fluid.
Electricity is the set of physical phenomena associated with the presence and motion of electric charge. In metals, the charge is carried by electrons.
Rubbing two materials together can transfer electrons from one to the other, leaving both charged. Charged objects attract or repel each other.
Materials are classed as conductors, such as metals, which let charge flow freely, or insulators, such as glass and rubber, which do not.
In 1752 Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment showed that lightning is electrical. Lightning rods, which he invented, still protect buildings.
Nerve cells send signals as electrical impulses called action potentials.
Electricity is used in medicine in devices such as defibrillators and pacemakers. Early electrotherapy claims for many disorders were mostly unfounded.
An electric current is a flow of charge. It drives motors, lighting and electronics.

reasons: Both cover friction, conductors and Franklin's lightning experiment.
Static electricity scores close behind but leaves out current, nerves and medicine.

alignments.label: What electricity is

britannica.quote: the operations of a very subtile fluid

wikipedia.quote: the presence and motion of electric charge

alignments.note: Something does flow, as the fluid theory said, but it is charge carried by particles, not a fluid of its own.

alignments.label: Friction

britannica.quote: excited by the friction of glass, amber, sealing-wax and other bodies

wikipedia.quote: Rubbing two materials together can transfer electrons

alignments.note: Rubbing still charges things. Today we know it moves electrons.

alignments.label: Attract and repel

britannica.quote: causes them to attract and repel light substances

wikipedia.quote: Charged objects attract or repel each other

alignments.note: The same observation in both texts.

alignments.label: Electrics and conductors

britannica.quote: electrics, which may be excited by friction, as glass and resin, and conductors, as metals and water

wikipedia.quote: conductors, such as metals, which let charge flow freely, or insulators, such as glass

alignments.note: The same division under a new name: the "electrics" are today’s insulators.

britannica.quote: Dr Franklin has shown that lightning is the same with electricity

wikipedia.quote: Benjamin Franklin's kite experiment showed that lightning is electrical

alignments.label: Electricity in medicine

britannica.quote: applied with success in medicine, in palsies, rheumatisms and other disorders

wikipedia.quote: Early electrotherapy claims for many disorders were mostly unfounded

alignments.note: Electricity did find a place in medicine, but not for the palsies and rheumatisms named here.

alignments.label: Nerves are electrical

britannica.quote: the nervous fluid itself may be of the same nature with the electric fluid

wikipedia.quote: Nerve cells send signals as electrical impulses

alignments.note: A guess in 1797, confirmed since: nerve signals are electrical.

alignments.label: Current and its uses

wikipedia.quote: An electric current is a flow of charge

alignments.note: The 1797 entry knows sparks and shocks, not steady current or electric power.

suggestedQuestions: Which of the 1797 claims about electricity turned out right?
What did the 1797 entry get wrong about electricity?

Which of the 1797 claims about electrici.answer:
Most of them. Friction excites it [B1], as rubbing transfers electrons [W2]. The split into electrics and conductors [B2] survives as insulators and conductors [W3]. Franklin’s proof that lightning is electrical [B3] still stands [W4].

Even the guess that the nervous fluid is electrical [B5] is now established: nerve cells signal with electrical impulses [W5].

What did the 1797 entry get wrong about.answer: Nothing outright, but two claims are only partly right. It calls electricity "a very subtile fluid" [B1]; today it is charge carried by electrons [W1]. And it says electricity was applied "with success" for palsies and rheumatisms [B4], while Wikipedia calls most early electrotherapy claims unfounded [W6].
